html:
The Poona Pact was an agreement signed on 24 September 1932 between B. R. Ambedkar and leaders of the caste Hindus, made while Gandhi was fasting in prison. It decided how the castes then called untouchable would be represented in India's legislatures.

In August 1932 the British government announced that the "Depressed Classes" would vote separately for their own members, as Muslims and Sikhs already did. Ambedkar had asked for this. He argued that an untouchable elected by a mostly caste-Hindu electorate would be a tool of the majority.

Gandhi, held in Yerwada jail at Pune, said separate electorates would split Hindu society for ever and leave untouchability in place. On 20 September he began a fast to the death. As he weakened, the pressure on Ambedkar was intense: if Gandhi died, there might be revenge on his people across India.

After four days of talks he signed. The separate electorate was dropped. In return the Depressed Classes got 148 reserved seats in the provincial legislatures, in place of 71, to be filled by all voters together.

Temples and wells were opened in the following weeks. Ambedkar later called the fast moral blackmail. The reserved seats of the Indian Constitution come from this pact.
